content: Superficial anatomy, also referred to as surface anatomy, is a branch of descriptive science that focuses on anatomical features observable by sight, without the need for dissection of an organism. Specifically, in the context of human anatomy, it involves the study of the form and proportions of the human body, as well as the surface landmarks that correspond to deeper structures not visible externally. These features can be examined both in static postures and during motion. This field is also known as visual anatomy. Furthermore, the discipline of superficial anatomy encompasses the theories and systems related to body proportions and their associated artistic canons. The study of superficial anatomy serves as the foundation for the accurate depiction of the human body in classical art. Additionally, certain pseudosciences, such as physiognomy, phrenology, and palmistry, rely on principles of superficial anatomy. However, the relationship between these pseudosciences and superficial anatomy is one-sided, akin to the relationship between astrology and astronomy. The study of superficial anatomy includes a catalog of external anatomical features, which are the visible parts of the body in both humans and animals. These features are generally organized in a cranial-to-caudal sequence. Homologous structures are grouped together and separated by commas, while subcomponents are nested within the main features. Alternative names or category members are provided in parentheses, and the class in which a component occurs is indicated in italics.
